Core Web Vitals answer that question with three metrics that focus on loading, reusability, and responsiveness. In this video, I will walk through each one and show you what is actually happening inside the browser.

Core Web Vitals focus on three aspects of user experience. The first one is Largest Contentful Paint or LCP, which measures how quickly the main content appears. The second one is Cumulative Layout Shift or CLS, which measures how stable the page layout is. And the third one is Interaction to Next Paint or INP,

which measures how responsive the page feels when user interactively visit. In this video, I will explain each of them with a short visual animation, and then we will look at the simple before and after code example to see how those issues usually happen in real applications. Let's start with Largest Contentful

Paint or LCP. LCP measures the time it takes for the largest visible element in the viewport to finish rendering. Usually, this element is something like a hero image, a large heading, or the main content block. So, instead of asking when did the page start loading, LCP asks a more meaningful question. When does the main content actually

appears for the user? For good user experience, Google recommend keeping LCP under 2.5 seconds. Let's visualize how the browser calculate this. larger element appears, so the browser update the candidate. Finally, the largest element appears on the screen, and once that element finish rendering, the browser records the LCP time. Largest Contentful Paint or LCP focuses on loading performance. The key idea is to make sure the most important content uh appears as early as possible.

Cumulative Layout Shift or CLS focuses on visual stability. We want the layout to remain stable while page loads. So, reserving space for images and the dynamic content is very important.
